# Exercise solutions

The following code relates to the exercises within the Preparation_and_editing_code.Rmd and Imputation_code.Rmd, within the Analysis for Action GitHub repository. Provided here are the solutions to the exercises.

## Troubleshooting

If you encounter any issues running the code snippets, consider the following
troubleshooting steps:
- Ensure you have followed the setup instructions in the
[README.md](../../../README.md) file including `install.packages()` for

# Packages and data

Before running the code snippets, ensure you have:
- followed the setup instructions in the [README.md](README.md) file,
- install the required packages
- run the code block below.


```{r setup, message=FALSE}
# Load in the following packages

library(tidyverse)
library(editrules)
library(deducorrect)
library(VIM)
library(mice)
library(lattice)
library(lme4)
library(igraph)
library(here)

# Load in data
# Use here::here() to construct paths, do not setwd()
here::here()
survey_data <- read_csv(here::here("Data","unclean_data.csv"))
clean_survey_data <- read_csv(here::here("Data","cleaned_data.csv"))
```

# Preparing and editing code
## Automatic editing exercise

1. Set a restriction on the days_unable_28d column in survey_data, where the column should have non-negative values and less than and equal to 28.

2. Using survey_data, check if the rules have been violated and assign it to variable violate.

3. Convert violate to a dataframe using data.frame() function.

4. Filter the rows where either of the edit rules have been violated.

5. Do the correction using the deducorrect package (Hint: the correction will be that wherever the days_unable_28d is greater than 100, divide it by 10).

```{r}

# Set the rule where days_unable_28d should be non-negative and less than and equal to 28

E <- editrules::editset(c("days_unable_28d >=0", "days_unable_28d <= 28"))

# Display the results

E


# Check if the rules are violated 

violate <- editrules::violatedEdits(E, dat = survey_data)

# Display first 6 rows

violate[1:6,]


# Convert violate to a dataframe 

violate_data <- data.frame(violate)

# Filter the rows where either of the edit rules have been violated
# Once you create a data frame you can see the column names by using $ sign

violate_data %>% 
dplyr::filter(num1 == TRUE | num2 == TRUE)
```
```{r}
# select records 145 and 376 record from the survey_data and the days_unable_28d column

survey_data[c(145,376),9]
```
```{r}
# Specify the rule and the correction 
# Since the restriction is that days_unable_28d should be non-negative and less than and equal to 28
# specify the rule that wherever days_unable_28d gain is greater than 28, divide it by 10

corr_rules <- deducorrect::correctionRules(expression(if(days_unable_28d > 28) {
      days_unable_28d <- days_unable_28d/10
}))

# Apply simple replacement rules to a data.frame.

corr <- deducorrect::correctWithRules(rules = corr_rules, dat = survey_data)

# list of alterations

corr$corrections

```

# Imputation 

## Mean imputation exercise

1. Using mice() function, impute the missing values in the clean_survey_data data.

2. Store the imputed data using the complete() function.

3. Look at the difference in the standard deviation of the hours_worked_away_7d column in imputed data and original data.

4. Impute the missing values for `hours_worked_away_7d` using mean imputation. 

```{r}

# Create a flag before imputation
hours_worked_away_7d_flag <- ifelse(is.na(clean_survey_data$hours_worked_away_7d), TRUE, FALSE)

# Perform mean imputation using MICE
mean_impute <- mice(clean_survey_data, method = 'mean', m = 1, maxit = 1)

# Store imputed data using complete() function
mean__data <- mice::complete(mean_impute) 

# Add the imputation flags
mean__data$hours_worked_away_7d_flag <- hours_worked_away_7d_flag


# Standard deviation of hours_worked_away_7d for original data 

sd(clean_survey_data$hours_worked_away_7d, na.rm = TRUE)

# Standard deviation of hours_worked_away_7d for imputed data 

sd(mean_data$hours_worked_away_7d, na.rm = TRUE)
```
The value for the imputed data, 17.08 (2dp) is lower than the original data, 17.53 (2dp). This is expected since mean imputation reduces the variance of the imputed variables because the imputation method adds more observations which are the mean - and so this reduces the average deviation from the mean for the data.


## Random hot deck imputation exercise

1. Carry out random hot deck imputation to impute the missing value in the general_health variable for the fifth person in the shorter data using the matching variable sex. Remember shorter data contains the first 10 observations from the clean_survey_data set.

```{r}
# Create a shorter data with 10 rows and all columns

shorter_data <- clean_survey_data[1:10,]

# Using hotdeck function in VIM package to carry out random hot deck imputation on general_health
# Sex as domain variable
VIM::hotdeck(data = shorter_data, variable = "general_health", domain_var = "sex" )
```

Here the potential imputed values could be 'Fair, 'Good' or 'Very Good'. 

## Sequential hot deck exercise

1. Carry out sequential hot deck imputation to impute the missing value in the general_health variable for the fifth person in the shorter data using the matching variables age_group while ordering the ethnic_group column. Remember shorter data contains the first 10 observations from the clean_survey_data data set.

```{r}

# Create a shorter data with 10 rows and all columns

shorter_data <- clean_survey_data[1:10,]

# Define age_group variable
shorter_data <- shorter_data |>
  mutate(age_group = case_when(
      age >= 18 & age <= 34 ~ "18-34",
      age >= 35 & age <= 49 ~ "35-49",
      age >= 50 & age <= 64 ~ "50-64",
      age >= 65 & age <= 79 ~ "65-79",
      age >= 80             ~ "80+",
      TRUE                  ~ NA_character_
    )
  )
```

```{r}

# Using hotdeck function in VIM package to carry out random hot deck imputation on general_health
# Sex as domain variable
VIM::hotdeck(data = shorter_data, variable = "general_health", 
             domain_var = "age_group",
             ord_var = "employment_status")
```

```{r}
# Arranging ethnic_group column in ascending order 

shorter_data %>% 
  dplyr::arrange(employment_status)
```

Therefore, the donor is P0002 and the imputed value is "Good".

## KNN Exercise 

1. Impute the missing value in the hours_worked_away_7d variable for the fifth person using K-Nearest Neighbours. Because all of the missing hours_worked_away_7d values in the dataset are among employed people, restrict the donor pool first to employed respondents only. Then use the 5 closest donors for kNN, and use days_unable_28d, sex and employment_status as distance variables.

```{r}

# Select employed respondents only
employed_data <- clean_survey_data |>
  dplyr::filter(employment_status == "Employed")

# Using KNN function in VIM package 
# k is the number of nearest neighbour donors used

knn_imputation_cont <- VIM::kNN(data = employed_data, variable = "hours_worked_away_7d", k = 5,
                                dist_var = c("days_unable_28d", "sex", "employment_status"))


# Display results

knn_imputation_cont %>% 
   dplyr::select("hours_worked_away_7d", everything()) %>%  
   head()

```
The imputed value in the hours_worked_away_7d column is chosen randomly using 5 closest donors.
